title: United Kingdom GP 2026: Practice, Sprint Qualifying Analysis & Weekend Predictions
summary: Hamilton takes sprint pole at home by eleven thousandths - and our exclusive aggregated FP1 data named that exact front row hours before Sprint Qualifying began. Inside: Ferrari's decisive Sector 3 advantage, McLaren's final-sector problem worth 0.739s, and Verstappen's hidden margin heading into Saturday.

sections.heading: The Verdict: Ferrari Own Silverstone, and FP1 Called It First
sections.content:
Lewis Hamilton takes sprint pole at home with a 1:28.376, eleven thousandths clear of Kimi Antonelli. That is the result. The more interesting story is that our aggregated FP1 data had already named that exact front row, in that exact order, several hours before Sprint Qualifying began - Hamilton first on 1:29.211, Antonelli second at +0.262. No official timing screen showed that. Ours did.

Four verdicts come out of Friday at Silverstone. First, Ferrari have the strongest single-lap car this weekend, and their advantage is concentrated in the final sector where Hamilton's 24.631 was the fastest of anyone by 0.080s. Second, McLaren are in trouble here in a way the SQ3 sheet flatters - Norris and Piastri qualified sixth and seventh, but the aggregated data shows their deficit is almost entirely a Sector 3 problem, not a general one. Third, Red Bull left the most on the table: Verstappen's FP1 aggregated lap was 0.187s quicker than anything he actually strung together, the largest untapped margin in the top six, and he converted it in Sprint Qualifying by jumping from fifth on aggregated pace to third on the grid.

Fourth, and least comfortable reading: Aston Martin are 4.5 seconds off sprint pole. Not four tenths. Four and a half seconds, with both cars out in SQ1 after five laps apiece. Their FP1 aggregated times - 1:32.881 and 1:32.890 - said the same thing before qualifying confirmed it.

Everything below is the evidence. The sprint grid, the exclusive aggregated-versus-actual breakdown, the sector-by-sector picture, the tyre allocations, and where all of it points for Saturday and Sunday.

sections.heading: Sprint Qualifying: Hamilton by Eleven Thousandths
sections.content:
SQ3 at Silverstone produced one of the tightest top-eight spreads of the season: 0.459s covered Hamilton in first from Isack Hadjar in eighth, with four different teams inside that window. Hamilton's 1:28.376 was the only lap in the 1:28.3s, and Antonelli's 1:28.387 was the closest anyone came to denying a home pole - the Mercedes rookie improved by 1.359s from his SQ1 benchmark, the biggest session-long gain of any driver who reached SQ3.

Behind them, Verstappen's 1:28.697 put Red Bull third and continued a pattern that has defined his season: he does not look quick on Friday runs, then produces the lap when the timing counts. Leclerc slotted in six thousandths behind at 1:28.703, meaning both Ferraris and both Mercedes were separated by less than four tenths in total. Russell's 1:28.733 was fifth, 0.346s adrift of his teammate - the second-largest intra-team gap among the front-runners after Ferrari's 0.327s.

McLaren were the surprise of the session, and not in a good way. Norris scraped through SQ1 with a 1:30.142 that was slower than eight cars, then rescued sixth on the grid with a 1:28.740 that arrived 1.402s better than where he started. Piastri was more orderly all session and ended up seventh, 0.032s behind Norris - the tightest teammate margin on the grid, and cold comfort given both papaya cars are behind three rival teams.

Racing Bulls provided the midfield headline. Lawson's 1:28.927 was genuinely quick for ninth, while Arvid Lindblad became the only driver to go slower in SQ3 than SQ2 - a 1:29.367 against his earlier 1:29.330. Pierre Gasly missed the cut by 0.152s, and Aston Martin's session ended in SQ1 with Alonso and Stroll 21st and 22nd, more than 4.5s off the pole benchmark.

sections.heading: FP1 Recap: One Session, and the Data Already Knew
sections.content:
Sprint weekends give teams exactly sixty minutes before parc fermé, which makes FP1 the single most valuable hour of the weekend - and makes what you can extract from it decisive. On aggregated pace, Hamilton headed the session at 1:29.211, built from a 28.403 opening sector on lap 25, a 36.177 middle sector three laps later, and a 24.631 final sector back on lap 25. Antonelli followed at 1:29.473 with all three of his best sectors coming on the same lap, then Leclerc at 1:29.687 and Russell at 1:29.938.

Compare that aggregated order against what happened in Sprint Qualifying and the correlation is striking. The eight fastest drivers on FP1 aggregated pace - Hamilton, Antonelli, Leclerc, Russell, Verstappen, Piastri, Hadjar, Norris - were the exact eight drivers who filled the top eight sprint grid slots. Not one interloper. The internal ordering shuffled, as it always does when fuel comes out and track evolution kicks in, but the identity of the fastest eight cars at Silverstone was established sixty minutes into the weekend.

The actual FP1 times told a slightly different and less useful story. Hamilton's fastest single lap was 1:29.260, Antonelli's 1:29.473, Leclerc's 1:29.859 and - critically - Verstappen's 1:30.240, which had him only sixth and looking ordinary. Anyone reading official timing on Friday afternoon would have written Red Bull off. The aggregated figure of 1:30.053 said something different: the pace was in the car, it just had not appeared on one lap yet.

The theoretical ultimate FP1 lap, taking the fastest sector from anyone on the grid, was 1:29.177 - Antonelli's 28.369 first sector bolted onto Hamilton's 36.177 and 24.631. Nobody was ever going to drive it, but it frames how narrow the true performance window was.

sections.heading: Hidden Potential: Aggregated vs Actual Lap Times (FP1)
sections.description: Exclusive analysis - each driver's personal best sectors combined into an ultimate lap, set against their fastest single complete lap. The delta is the time they had available but never assembled.

sections.heading: Understanding Aggregated vs Actual Times
sections.content:
An aggregated lap is a driver's fastest first sector, fastest second sector and fastest third sector from the session, added together regardless of which lap each came from. Hamilton's 1:29.211 does not exist in the timing logs as a lap he drove - his best middle sector came on lap 28, three laps after the other two. It is what his car and his driving were capable of on Friday, assembled from evidence rather than from luck.

That matters because qualifying is precisely the exercise of putting all three sectors together at once. In practice, drivers are managing fuel loads, traffic, tyre preparation and set-up experiments, and a scruffy middle sector ruins an otherwise representative lap. Come Sprint Qualifying or Q3, the traffic is managed, the tyre is prepared and the fuel is minimal - so the aggregated number is a better forecast of where a car will end up than the actual number is.

Read the delta as an execution score. A figure near zero, like Antonelli's, Russell's or Norris's flat 0.000, means the driver's best lap already was their optimal lap - everything the car had, on one lap. A large delta, like Verstappen's +0.187 or Hulkenberg's +0.228, means the pace exists but arrived in pieces. Those are the drivers who tend to move up between Friday and Saturday.

This breakdown is not published by F1.com or any official timing feed, which report only completed laps. Reconstructing it requires lap-level sector data for every driver across every run - which is what this platform exists to do.

sections.heading: Sector-by-Sector: Where Silverstone Is Won
sections.content:
Silverstone splits neatly into three character tests, and Friday's sector data shows three different cars winning them. Sector 1 - Abbey, Farm Curve, Village, the Loop and Aintree - went to Antonelli at 28.369, with Hamilton 0.034s back and Russell third on 28.447. That combination of a flat-out opening complex and a heavy braking, low-speed loop rewards the Mercedes' front-end stability, and the W17 has been the reference through this stretch all weekend.

Sector 2 carries the Wellington Straight, Brooklands, Luffield, then Copse and the Maggotts–Becketts–Chapel sequence: the most demanding high-speed direction changes on the calendar. Hamilton's 36.177 led it, ahead of Antonelli's 36.209 and Leclerc's 36.233 - three cars covered by 0.056s, and evidence that Ferrari and Mercedes are running comparable aerodynamic efficiency through fast corners.

Sector 3 is where the weekend is actually being decided. Hamilton's 24.631 through Stowe, Vale and Club was 0.080s clear of Leclerc's 24.711 - a Ferrari one-two in the sector that rewards traction out of slow corners and stability under heavy braking. Everyone else is a long way back. Verstappen managed 24.920, Russell 25.078, and Norris - fourth fastest in Sector 1 - could only produce 25.370.

That Norris number is the most revealing figure in the dataset. Of his 1.077s aggregated deficit to Hamilton, 0.739s comes from Sector 3 alone; he loses just 0.105s in Sector 1. Piastri shows the same signature, giving up 0.473s of his 0.853s deficit in the final sector. McLaren's problem at Silverstone is not downforce or top speed - it is what the car does on the exit of Club corner. One curiosity for the anoraks: Valtteri Bottas's Cadillac posted a 25.365 final sector, five thousandths faster than Norris's McLaren.

sections.heading: Tyre Strategy: A Sprint Weekend Spent Sparingly
sections.content:
Sprint weekends compress the tyre picture, and the split in FP1 was clean along competitive lines. Ferrari, Mercedes, McLaren and Red Bull all ran a soft-plus-hard programme in the hour - one qualifying simulation, one long run on the hard - while Alpine, Audi and Lawson's Racing Bulls skipped the soft entirely and worked through a medium and two hards. That is the difference between teams confident of their single-lap pace and teams needing race data.

Sprint Qualifying followed the mandated compound sequence: mediums in SQ1 and SQ2, softs reserved for SQ3. The ten drivers who reached SQ3 each burned a fresh soft for it; the six eliminated in SQ2 - Gasly, Bortoleto, Hulkenberg, Colapinto, Sainz and Albon - got through two mediums and kept their softs intact. Aston Martin, Cadillac and Haas used just a single medium apiece before their SQ1 elimination, which is the one silver lining in an otherwise bleak Friday for them.

Norris stands out for volume. Twelve sets used across the weekend so far, seven of them softs, is the highest count in the field - two softs in FP1 alone, where every other front-runner managed with one. Burning that much rubber and emerging sixth on the sprint grid suggests McLaren were chasing a set-up answer rather than banking a result. At the other end, Colapinto, Stroll, Ocon and Perez have used seven sets each.

For the sprint itself, the front-running teams have a medium earmarked for the seventeen-lap run, while Alonso and Bottas are the only two with a soft set aside - a low-risk gamble from cars with nothing to lose from the back rows. Everyone else keeps three to five softs in hand for Saturday's main qualifying.

sections.heading: Sprint Race Predictions
sections.content:
**Sprint podium prediction:** 1. Hamilton (Ferrari) - pole, the strongest final sector on the grid and the hardest car on this circuit to pass. 2. Antonelli (Mercedes) - quick enough to threaten into Abbey on lap one, but Mercedes' Sector 3 deficit of 0.264s makes a pass stick only if it happens immediately. 3. Verstappen (Red Bull) - starts third, has the largest untapped margin in the field and the least to lose in a race with no pit stops.

**Sprint strategy:** Seventeen laps, no mandatory stop, and the medium is the obvious choice for everyone with track position to protect - which is precisely what the allocation data shows the front-runners holding. Degradation over such a short run is a non-issue at Silverstone; tyre temperature in the opening two laps is the real variable, and the cars starting on the dirty side of the grid will spend the first sector fighting for grip.

**Sprint wildcard:** Leclerc. Fourth on the grid with the second-fastest final sector of anyone, he has the one weapon that matters here - traction onto the run to the line. If he clears Verstappen early, a Ferrari one-two is live.

**Key sprint battle:** Norris versus Piastri, sixth against seventh, separated by 0.032s. McLaren's cars are equally matched, equally frustrated and equally aware that finishing behind three rival teams is unacceptable in a title year. Expect a scrap that costs both of them time relative to the cars ahead.

sections.heading: Qualifying & Race Day Predictions
sections.content:
**Qualifying prediction (built on aggregated FP1 data):** In qualifying, drivers assemble all three sectors - which is exactly what the aggregated numbers already measure. Hamilton led that order on Friday and converted it into sprint pole, and with an additional day of rubber laid down we expect pole to fall around 1:28.0. Predicted top three: Hamilton, Antonelli, Leclerc, following the aggregated standings rather than the sprint result. The caveat carries a name: Verstappen. His +0.187 delta was the largest untapped margin among the front-runners, and a driver who improves in Q3 more reliably than anyone on the grid is a genuine threat to that front row.

**Untapped potential to watch:** Hulkenberg's +0.228 and Lawson's +0.221 are the biggest deltas outside the top ten in Friday's order. Hulkenberg's Audi was ninth on aggregated FP1 pace but only thirteenth in Sprint Qualifying - a conversion failure rather than a pace deficit, and one Audi can fix overnight.

**Race prediction:** Hamilton to win. Ferrari's Sector 3 advantage is a defensive weapon at a circuit where the final sector feeds straight onto the pit straight and DRS detection, and the medium-to-hard one-stop is comfortably the fastest route through 52 laps. Expect the majority of the field to start on the medium and switch to the hard between laps 18 and 24, with anyone starting on the soft committed to a two-stop and an early undercut attempt.

**Podium prediction:** 1. Hamilton (Ferrari), 2. Verstappen (Red Bull), 3. Antonelli (Mercedes).

**Wildcard factors:** This is Silverstone in July, which means the forecast is a genuine strategic variable rather than a footnote. A ten-minute shower over Stowe reshuffles everything, and the safety car probability sits around 40% given the Abbey and Copse traffic patterns at the start.

**Dark horse:** Hadjar. Eighth on the sprint grid, +0.094 delta showing a driver already extracting what the car has, and a Sector 1 time within 0.006s of Verstappen's. If Red Bull's race pace is as strong as their Friday potential suggested, a top-five finish is well within range.

**Key battle to watch:** Hamilton versus Antonelli, past and future Mercedes, separated by eleven thousandths on Friday. It is the fight of the weekend, and it will be decided in the last sector.
